title: The Best AI Thought Pieces I've Encountered Recently
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. curates four AI-related thought pieces he found valuable — a video on "How Will AI Change Education?", an Ezra Klein/Rebecca Winthrop conversation on parenting and education, a skeptical math educator's short take on inflated AI-in-education claims, and a broader Tristan Harris warning about AI echoing his earlier social-media warnings — before pivoting to his own argument. He singles out the first video's core question, "How do we force learners to care about learning?", to argue that forcing care is impossible but cultivating it is the real task, and that Moments of Genuine Connection alone won't get students to value laborious learning work. His "My Take" section directly criticizes schools for "hopping onto the AI bandwagon recklessly" on the grounds that students will need AI skills for future jobs, calling that reasoning misguided given how unpredictable the technology's trajectory has already proven. He grounds his skepticism in his own track record of misjudging AI (having once dismissed ChatGPT as "no thing but a chicken wing") and argues that AI use is not a generic, transferable skill but one entirely dependent on a user's underlying domain knowledge. The piece closes by reasserting that developing students' actual competence and character remains the goal AI should serve, not replace.
points: Stuart calls out the framing question "How do we force learners to care about learning?" from a video he recommends, arguing the premise is wrong — you can't force care, only cultivate it.
His central objection to reckless school AI adoption is the "future jobs" justification, which he calls misguided given how unpredictable AI's trajectory has already proven.
He cites his own past misjudgment — dismissing ChatGPT as "no thing but a chicken wing" — as evidence that confident predictions about AI's educational impact deserve skepticism.

His key pedagogical claim is that AI use is not a generic, transferable skill but is entirely dependent on a user's domain knowledge, which raises rather than lowers the stakes of building student expertise.
He flags the Tristan Harris piece as notable for extending his earlier social-media warnings to AI, the only recommended piece not specific to education.
quotes: THEN he gets into potential applications for AI in education, and the core dilemma he lands on by the end is, "How do we force learners to care about learning?
Except that he's wrong to ask how to force learners to care — you can't do that. But you can cultivate care.

Schools around the nation are hopping onto the AI bandwagon recklessly. We use arguments like, "We've got to get our kids using AI because this is what their future jobs will require." Frankly, this is misguided.
AI use, like critical thinking, is not a generic skill but is dependent on a user's understanding of the domain they are using AI in.
We want our students to become as smart and capable and good as they can become. AI doesn't diminish that objective; rather, it increases its importance and urgency.
